medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.prompt: A resident reports chest tightness and has nitroglycerin ordered SL. The tablet is in the med cart. What should the medication aide do?

options.a: Place the tablet under the tongue and tell the resident not to swallow it whole
options.b: Crush the tablet into applesauce so it will not worsen the chest tightness
options.c: Have the resident swallow it with a full glass of water like a regular PO pill
options.d: Press the tablet onto intact chest skin as if it were a small transdermal patch

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.explanation: Sublingual nitroglycerin is absorbed under the tongue. Swallowing it as a PO tablet delays or blocks that effect. Do not crush it or apply it to skin. Coach the resident to let it dissolve and not to chew or wash it down with water unless the product directions say otherwise.

distractorExplanations.b: Crushing SL nitroglycerin changes the dose delivery; it is not mixed into food for oral swallow.
distractorExplanations.c: A full glass of water is the oral (PO) route; SL means under the tongue until dissolved, not swallowed whole.
distractorExplanations.d: Transdermal patches go on skin; an SL tablet is not a chest patch and will not absorb that way.

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.prompt: Swallow notes say the resident chokes on whole tablets. The next dose is enteric-coated aspirin. What is the correct action?

options.a: Crush the tablet finely and mix it in pudding so the resident can swallow it
options.b: Leave the coating intact; hold the dose and ask the nurse about another form
options.c: Split the tablet in half so each piece is easier to swallow than the whole
options.d: Soak off the coating in hot water, then give the liquid through a straw

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.explanation: Enteric coating protects the stomach and times release in the intestine. Crushing, splitting, or dissolving it dumps the dose early and can irritate the gut. If the resident cannot swallow the tablet whole, hold and ask the nurse about a liquid or other ordered form—do not improvise a crush.

distractorExplanations.a: Crushing enteric-coated aspirin destroys the coating; that is a common swallow-risk shortcut, not an allowed change of form.
distractorExplanations.c: Splitting still breaks the enteric coat on many products; it is not a safe substitute for an intact tablet.
distractorExplanations.d: Hot water dissolving the coat is the same error as crushing: the delayed-release design is gone.

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.prompt: A transdermal pain patch is due. Yesterday's patch is still on the other arm. How should the aide apply the new patch?

options.a: Place the new patch over the old one so the doses overlap without a gap
options.b: Rub lotion on the site first so the adhesive holds through a full wear period
options.c: Remove the old patch, date the new one, and apply it to clean dry intact skin
options.d: Stick every new patch on the same site so absorption stays as consistent as possible

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.explanation: Two patches on at once stack the dose. Remove the old patch, dispose of it per policy, and apply the new one to clean, dry, intact skin in a rotated site. Date and initial as trained. Lotions and oils block adhesion and can change how much drug the skin takes up.

distractorExplanations.a: Leaving the old patch on and adding a new one double-doses; the used patch must come off first.
distractorExplanations.b: Lotion and oil under a patch reduce stick and can alter absorption; the skin should be clean and dry.
distractorExplanations.d: Sites are rotated to limit irritation; reusing one spot is not how consistent absorption is maintained.

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.prompt: Two different ophthalmic drops are due in the same eye this morning. What technique should the medication aide use?

options.a: Drop both medicines onto the cornea so they absorb before the resident blinks
options.b: Give the second drop immediately so neither medicine rinses the first one away
options.c: Borrow the roommate's bottle when the drug name and strength match exactly
options.d: Place drops in the lower sac, keep the tip off the eye, and wait between drugs

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.explanation: Eye drops go into the lower conjunctival sac, not onto the cornea. Keep the dropper from touching the eye or lashes so the bottle stays clean. Wait several minutes (about five is a common teaching) between different drops so the second does not wash out the first. Bottles are single-resident items.

distractorExplanations.a: The cornea is sensitive and triggers blinking; drops belong in the lower conjunctival sac.
distractorExplanations.b: Back-to-back drops wash the first drug out; wait between different ophthalmic products as trained.
distractorExplanations.c: Sharing eye-drop bottles spreads infection even when the printed names match.

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.prompt: A resident is due a metered-dose inhaler and an inhaled corticosteroid. Which technique is correct?

options.a: Shake when required, coach a slow breath, then rinse after the steroid
options.b: Fire both puffs back to back with no pause so the lungs get a stacked dose
options.c: Skip the mouth rinse after the steroid unless the resident asks for a drink
options.d: Share one spacer on the hall if it is wiped with alcohol between residents

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.explanation: Device technique is the dose. Shake or prime when the product requires it, time a slow deep breath as taught, and wait between puffs when the label says to. Rinse or spit after an inhaled steroid to cut oral thrush risk. Spacers stay with one resident; wiping does not make sharing safe.

distractorExplanations.b: Most MDI labels call for a short wait between puffs; stacking them immediately is poor technique.
distractorExplanations.c: Rinsing after a steroid inhaler is part of the technique, not an optional comfort sip.
distractorExplanations.d: Spacers are single-resident devices; alcohol wipe-downs do not justify sharing.

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.prompt: A glycerin rectal suppository is ordered. How should the medication aide administer it?

options.a: Keep the foil wrapper on so the aide can insert it without touching the drug
options.b: Unwrap it, keep privacy, and insert as trained in left side-lying
options.c: Soften it in warm water and have the resident swallow it like an oral gelcap
options.d: Insert it with the resident on the right side so it follows the sigmoid colon

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.explanation: A rectal suppository is unwrapped and inserted into the rectum as trained, with privacy and gloves. The usual adult position is left side-lying (Sims') so the product follows colon anatomy. Foil left on blocks melting. It is never given by mouth; if too soft, chill briefly rather than soaking it.

distractorExplanations.a: The wrapper must come off; foil in the rectum cannot melt or be absorbed.
distractorExplanations.c: Rectal products are not swallowed; warming in water and giving PO is the wrong route.
distractorExplanations.d: Right-side lying is the common mix-up; adult teaching is left Sims' for rectal insertion.

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.prompt: A tablet is ordered buccal. The resident lifts a cup to swallow it with water. What should the aide do?

options.a: Let the resident swallow it; buccal and oral routes work the same after a sip
options.b: Move the tablet under the tongue instead, because buccal means sublingual
options.c: Crush it and pack the powder in the cheek so it dissolves faster than whole
options.d: Place it between cheek and gum and tell the resident not to swallow it yet

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.explanation: Buccal means between the cheek and gum until the tablet dissolves. Swallowing it turns it into a PO dose and can blunt the intended absorption. Sublingual is under the tongue, a different site. Do not crush a buccal tablet unless the order and product allow a change of form.

distractorExplanations.a: A sip that swallows the tablet is the oral route; buccal stays in the cheek pouch.
distractorExplanations.b: Under the tongue is sublingual; buccal is the cheek-and-gum pocket, not SL.
distractorExplanations.c: Crushing is not the buccal technique and can dump the dose unless the label allows it.

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.prompt: A liquid antibiotic is ordered 10 mL by mouth. How should the medication aide measure the dose?

options.a: Draw it in an oral syringe or pour it to the line on a marked medicine cup
options.b: Use a household teaspoon from the kitchen, counting it as about 10 milliliters
options.c: Fill the plastic bottle cap to the rim, treating that volume as a 10 mL dose
options.d: Use a leftover IM syringe with the needle off so the milliliter marks still match

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.explanation: Oral liquids are measured with a marked medicine cup or a dedicated oral syringe. Kitchen spoons and unmarked caps vary too much to be a dose. Parenteral syringes, even with the needle removed, invite wrong-route errors; keep oral devices for PO liquids.

distractorExplanations.b: Household teaspoons are not calibrated; volumes vary and under- or overdosing is likely.
distractorExplanations.c: A bottle cap has no dose line; filling to the rim is guessing, not measuring.
distractorExplanations.d: Injection syringes for oral liquids are a classic wrong-route trap; use an oral syringe.

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.prompt: Hydrocortisone cream is ordered to intact skin on the forearm. How should the aide apply it?

options.a: Spread a thick layer so the cream lasts until the next scheduled application
options.b: Glove or use an applicator and apply a thin layer only to the ordered site
options.c: Dip a bare finger in the jar and also rub cream into a nearby open skin tear
options.d: Cover the whole arm, including broken skin, so none of the irritation is missed

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.explanation: Topical cream is a thin film on the ordered intact site, with gloves or an applicator so the jar is not contaminated. A thick coat does not make the drug last longer and can overdose the skin. Open wounds need their own wound-care order; do not extend the cream there.

distractorExplanations.a: Thick layers waste product and can increase systemic or local exposure; apply thinly as ordered.
distractorExplanations.c: Bare-finger double-dipping contaminates a multi-use jar; open tears are not the ordered site.
distractorExplanations.d: Spreading onto broken skin is extra treatment without an order, not complete coverage.

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.prompt: The MAR lists a crushed tablet via NG tube. State rules and facility policy do not allow this aide to give tube meds. What should the aide do?

options.a: Crush the tablet, flush the tube with water, and give the dose to stay on time
options.b: Push the dry tablet into the tube and ask the nurse to check placement later
options.c: Hold the dose and ask the nurse; do not give NG meds outside allowed scope
options.d: Flush with cola only, because carbonation is thought to keep the tube from clogging

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.explanation: NG or gastrostomy meds are allowed only when the state and the facility say the medication aide may give them, and then only with the nurse's procedure (flush, form, placement checks). If tube route is out of scope, hold and notify the nurse. Do not crush-and-push to stay on time. Not every tablet may be crushed even when tube meds are allowed.

distractorExplanations.a: Giving via NG to keep the clock is practicing outside scope when policy forbids tube meds.
distractorExplanations.b: A dry tablet in the tube clogs and can misplace; it also skips the required nurse procedure.
distractorExplanations.d: Cola flushes are not a standing MA workaround and do not legalize an out-of-scope tube dose.

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.prompt: A resident's nasal corticosteroid spray is due. How should the medication aide aim the spray?

options.a: Aim the tip straight at the septum so the spray stays inside the nostril
options.b: Aim toward the back of the throat so the resident swallows the full labeled dose
options.c: Use one unit bottle for both roommates when they share the same spray order
options.d: Aim as labeled: usually the outer wall, not a hard blast at the septum

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.explanation: Most nasal sprays are aimed slightly outward, away from the septum, so the lining gets the dose and the septum is less likely to bleed. A hard midline blast irritates cartilage. Swallowing the spray is the wrong site. Bottles stay with one resident.

distractorExplanations.a: Straight at the septum is a nosebleed risk; teaching is usually toward the lateral wall.
distractorExplanations.b: Nasal sprays act on nasal mucosa; aiming so the dose is swallowed wastes the drug.
distractorExplanations.c: Shared nasal bottles spread infection even when two residents have matching orders.

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.prompt: A nurse draws up IM vitamin B12 and asks the medication aide to inject it because the floor is short-staffed. What should the aide do?

options.a: Refuse; IM injections are usually outside medication-aide scope
options.b: Give it if the resident consents, because consent expands the aide's legal scope
options.c: Give it because watching the nurse draw the syringe counts as IM competency
options.d: Give it if the nurse stays in the doorway, since the nurse remains responsible

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.explanation: In most states, medication aides do not give IM or IV medications as an independent action. Staffing pressure, resident consent, observation, or a nurse standing nearby does not add that route. The aide should refuse, leave the injection to licensed nursing, and follow the chain of command if pressured.

distractorExplanations.b: Consent to treatment does not rewrite state scope; the resident cannot authorize an IM by an MA.
distractorExplanations.c: Watching a draw-up is not competency or a license to inject intramuscularly.
distractorExplanations.d: Nurse presence does not transfer IM authority to the aide; the injection stays a nursing task.

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.prompt: A resident cannot swallow a whole extended-release capsule. The label does not say the beads may be sprinkled. What should the aide do?

options.a: Open it and mix the beads in applesauce so the resident can swallow them
options.b: Crush the beads with a pestle so the powder mixes evenly through pudding
options.c: Cut the capsule in half so each smaller piece is easier to swallow than whole
options.d: Leave it closed; hold the dose and ask the nurse about a swallowable form

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.explanation: Opening or crushing an XR/SR capsule dumps a timed dose at once unless the specific product labeling allows sprinkle. If the resident cannot swallow it whole and the label is silent, hold and ask the nurse about another form. Do not cut, crush, or open on a swallow-risk guess.

distractorExplanations.a: Sprinkling is allowed only when that capsule's labeling says so; applesauce is not a blanket OK.
distractorExplanations.b: Crushing beads destroys extended release and can cause a peak dose all at once.
distractorExplanations.c: Cutting the shell still breaks the release system on products that must be swallowed intact.

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.prompt: An adult resident has otic drops due in the left ear. How should the medication aide position the ear?

options.a: Pull the pinna down and back, using the same cue taught for a toddler's canal
options.b: Pull the pinna up and back for adults, with the affected ear facing up
options.c: Insert the dropper tip deep into the canal so none of the drops run back out
options.d: Keep the head level and facing forward so the drops coat only the outer ear

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.explanation: In adults, the pinna is pulled up and back to straighten the canal; young children are taught down and back. Tilt the affected ear up and keep it there a few minutes. The dropper stays outside the canal so it does not injure skin or contaminate the bottle.

distractorExplanations.a: Down and back is the pediatric cue; adults need up and back, not the toddler method.
distractorExplanations.c: Deep insertion can trauma the canal and seed the bottle; drops are instilled from outside.
distractorExplanations.d: A level head lets drops run out; the affected ear is kept up so the canal fills.

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.prompt: A saline lock is in place and the MAR shows an IV antibiotic due. The resident asks the aide to “just push it.” What should the aide do?

options.a: Push the dose if the nurse already mixed the bag, because mixing is the hard step
options.b: Start the IV push if the aide has given the same drug by mouth on other shifts
options.c: Hold and notify the nurse; IV medication is not independent MA practice
options.d: Connect the tubing if a licensed nurse later signs the MAR for the aide's push

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.explanation: IV (and IM) administration is not an independent medication-aide action in most states. A lock in place, a mixed bag, prior PO doses of the same drug, or a promised co-signature does not create IV authority. Hold, do not access the lock, and get a nurse.

distractorExplanations.a: Pharmacy or nurse mixing does not authorize the aide to push or hang IV medication.
distractorExplanations.b: PO experience with a drug is a different route; it does not qualify the aide for IV push.
distractorExplanations.d: A later MAR signature cannot legalize an out-of-scope IV push the aide already performed.
